evidence_quotes.quote: It is within this context that CBWRM has been identified as one of the approaches through which sustainable access and use of potable water resources and CD in rural communities of North-western Cameroon is promoted.
This paper examines the role of community-based water resource management in community development in Cameroon.

In addition, women were levied 500 FCFA (US1$) and men 1000 FCFA (US2$) for the realization of the water systems while maintenance fees were based on the gravity of the problem in the various localities.

A pilot survey was also conducted between the 2 of March 2015 to the 16 March, 2015 in Mbengwi, Njinikom and Ndu Municipalities (see Figure 1). From these three municipalities, two rural communities were randomly selected giving a total of six study sites: Tugi, Zang-Tabi, Baicham, Muloin, Njimkang and Ngarum, respectively.

The purpose of these interviews was to assess the institutional and policy frameworks that exist in the management of potable water in Cameroon and how this affects CD. Finally, preliminary discussions with five community leaders identified through key informants were conducted. In addition to these discussions, informal conversations with 10 households who were randomly selected were carried out with the aim of having an idea of how the community relate to water issues and CD.

Because of the long distances that we have to walk as women to get water which is even not of good quality, we have now formed a woman’s community group with the aim of helping members of the community to realise the village water project.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural potable water supply and community-based pipe-borne water schemes across six rural communities in North-west Cameroon.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2, which would include broad institutional or governance factors (community-based water resource management [CBWRM], CBOs, Village Development Associations, Water Management Committees, and state-community decentralization), so plain_criterion2_decision is 'include'. However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2: the paper focuses on generic participatory project delivery, grassroots solidarity in mobilizing self-help community development projects, and broad macro-governance/decentralization rhetoric rather than empirically analyzing a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, enforcement, regulatory structure, or tariff/cost-recovery rules as determinants of household access, affordability, or exclusion). Passing mentions of the 1998 water law (via secondary citation) and flat capital levies/maintenance fees serve only as unanalysed background or illustrations of community participation in building village schemes.
criterion_notes.c3: Combines a narrative literature review (61 selected articles/reports on CBNRM in sub-Saharan Africa) with primary qualitative empirical data from a March 2015 pilot study in six rural communities (interviews with 7 national ministry officials and 6 regional officials, preliminary discussions with 5 community leaders, informal conversations with 10 randomly selected households, and focus group discussions with women and youth).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative community- and household-level accounts of water shortages, long walking distances to poor-quality water sources, and the establishment/realization of community pipe-borne water projects (alongside secondary WHO/UNICEF JMP rural access figures), although the main analytical focus is community participation and community development.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (six rural communities—Tugi, Zang-Tabi, Baicham, Muloin, Njimkang, and Ngarum—in Mbengwi, Njinikom, and Ndu municipalities, with official, leader, household, and focus-group respondents), exposure (participatory CBWRM through CBOs, VDAs, and WMCs), qualitative outcomes, and qualitative pilot case-study design are identifiable.

study_design: Literature review combined with a qualitative participatory pilot study (key-informant interviews, informal household conversations, and focus group discussions)
population_and_sample: Six rural communities (Tugi, Zang-Tabi, Baicham, Muloin, Njimkang, and Ngarum) across Mbengwi, Njinikom, and Ndu municipalities in North-west Cameroon; pilot sample of 7 national ministry officials, 6 regional officials, 5 community leaders, 10 randomly selected households, and focus group participants (women and youth)
exposure: Community-based water resource management (CBWRM) and grassroots participation in self-help water project mobilization via CBOs, Village Development Associations (VDAs), and Water Management Committees (WMCs)
outcome: Community development, grassroots participation, and qualitative accounts of village water project realization, water shortages, and walking distances to water sources
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the paper discusses rural potable water supply in North-west Cameroon using a literature review and a two-week qualitative pilot study, its exposure is generic participatory community-based natural resource management (CBNRM/CBWRM), grassroots self-help project mobilization, and broad decentralization/community-development background rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or tariff mechanism directly governing service access. Brief references to the 1998 water law and community construction levies/maintenance fees are descriptive background for community solidarity rather than empirically analyzed rules governing household water access, affordability, or exclusion. Under the broader plain wording of Criterion 2, it would be included as a qualitative empirical study of community water governance.
